video_title: MacroVoices #557 Michael Every: The Blue Tsunami Lands on Markets... and Geopolitics
gist: Rabobank's Michael Every argues the Democrats' 2026 midterm sweep of both houses is a geopolitical shock that constrains the US as global policeman, widening the range of outcomes, and that markets are pricing too much optimism: the post-election $18 oil drop ignores likely Russia-Ukraine and possibly Iran escalation, keeping crack spreads and energy prices elevated. Patrick Ceresna adds that bonds and the dollar did not confirm a macro regime shift, the AI infrastructure/semis trade keeps breaking down while hyperscalers rally, gold's bounce looks like an oversold counter-trend, and proposes an MPC bull call spread on refining margins.

themes.theme: Blue sweep constrains US as global policeman

insights.claim: Michael Every argues the under-appreciated consequence of the Democrats winning both houses of Congress in the 2026 midterms is a global geopolitical shock, because a Congress opposed to foreign adventures makes the US a greatly constrained geopolitical actor.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Geopolitical risk premia globally may need repricing as US power projection becomes politically constrained.
insights.quote: what happens in America doesn't stay in America

insights.claim: Every says the new Congress's real constraint on the Iran war starts after January when it sits, and that prosecuting a Middle East war without backing of Congress or the public makes success enormously harder even if constitutional limits remain unsettled.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: January 2027 is a key date when US war-making capacity may shift, a catalyst for energy and defense markets.

insights.claim: Every lays out a spectrum where a US exit from the Middle East ('the ultimate taco') leaves a power vacuum filled either by Iran aligned with Russia, China and North Korea, or contested by Israel and Turkey, and argues neither scenario supports lower energy prices in the short term.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Peace-driven oil sell-offs may be mispriced since every withdrawal path keeps energy supply risk elevated.
insights.quote: In neither case at least short term does that make an argument for lower energy prices?

insights.claim: Every views an Israeli nuclear escalation as an extremely fat-tail risk, citing that even in the 1973 Yom Kippur war Golda Meir did not use nuclear weapons, and that Israel likely lacks tactical nuclear weapons.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Investors need not price nuclear escalation as a meaningful scenario despite US support possibly waning.
insights.quote: I still think that's an extremely fat tail risk and nothing more than that

insights.claim: Every hypothesizes that if the US and Israeli militaries decouple, Israel would seek new allies such as India, which offers large-scale production capacity and wants Israeli tech, and which would itself restrain Israeli nuclear brinkmanship.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Potential realignment of Israeli defense-tech partnerships toward India is a second-order theme for defense supply chains.

insights.claim: Every argues that if courts or Congress establish that Congress can stop a president's wars, the world will see a 1920s-style isolationist US, prompting powers without such domestic checks to fill gaps, which he calls an enormous potential geopolitical shock.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: A Congress-vs-president war-powers showdown could be a volatility catalyst the market is not pricing.
insights.quote: 100 years ago very isolationist 1920s US rather than 2020s

insights.claim: Every says the US-built world system, created by US military power in WWII and military plus financial power in the Cold War, is crumbling, and will collapse further if a deindustrialized US cannot sustain its military-industrial complex, causing 'international crime rates' to soar.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Structural case for higher geopolitical risk premia, defense spending by others, and supply-chain fragmentation.
insights.quote: if there is no cop on the beat, you know, which households in the international sense are believers in the Second Amendment and which ones aren't

insights.claim: Every argues US voters' lesson from the midterms is not opposition to all intervention but to wars that are not won quickly, contrasting the poorly received Iran war with the Venezuela operation that was over in two or three days with minimal bloodshed.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Future US interventions are likely to be short, decisive operations rather than prolonged campaigns.
insights.quote: It's doing it and not winning or not winning quickly.

insights.claim: Every contends that being anti-war does not prevent war for a hegemon, and that voting against wars will not by itself deliver lower energy prices without giving up major geostrategic advantage.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Political de-escalation narratives should not be equated with durable supply normalization.
insights.quote: being anti-war doesn't prevent war

themes.theme: Iran and Russia-Ukraine escalation risk to energy

insights.claim: Every's base case for months was that after the midterms Trump would escalate against Iran to finish the job before the new Congress sits, with more forces staged in Saudi Arabia and French and British jets there protecting Yanbu and Riyadh.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: The lame-duck window before January is a period of elevated Middle East escalation risk that oil has just discounted.

insights.claim: Every says the midterm defeat raises the chance Trump instead does a token action and retreats ('taco slash the whole enchilada'), but stresses that even this would not bring energy prices down sustainably.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Both escalation and retreat paths leave a floor under energy prices.
insights.quote: I don't think that is going to bring energy prices down sustainably the way that the US would like to see

insights.claim: Every argues Putin has little reason to deal in US-led Russia-Ukraine negotiations now, since Trump will be even weaker six months from now, making escalation more probable than peace.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Russia-Ukraine peace optimism looks premature; escalation risk to Russian energy infrastructure is rising.
insights.quote: Trump will be even weaker six months from now

insights.claim: Every says the best achievable Russia-Ukraine outcome is a frozen conflict in the North Korea-South Korea style, which still requires US backing and both sides' agreement.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Caps the upside of any peace trade; a full settlement is not the realistic endpoint.

insights.claim: Every says a US pullback means more Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which 'can only be bullish' for refining crack spreads, and that escalation on both the Russia-Ukraine and Middle East fronts would keep crack spreads and energy prices high.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Refiners and diesel cracks are a favored expression of the continued-conflict view.
insights.quote: It can only be bullish for that particular crack spread.

insights.claim: Erik Townsend argues that refinery strikes anywhere reduce global refining capacity, so crack spreads would stay dramatically elevated for years after the war ends.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Refining margin tailwind could persist beyond any ceasefire, supporting refiners structurally.
insights.quote: crack spreads will stay elevated, dramatically elevated for years after the war is over

insights.claim: Every says crude prices fell hugely in the two days after the election on a belief that Middle East peace is imminent, which he views as more optimism than realism.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Post-election oil weakness may be a buying opportunity if peace does not materialize.
insights.quote: I think there's an enormous amount of optimism rather than realism in terms of what that short-term move has done

insights.claim: Patrick Ceresna says oil fell about $18 peak-to-trough from Friday's peak to the day after the election, almost entirely risk premium removal with no meaningful change in fundamentals, and likens it to the Liberation Day equity overshoot that later rebounded.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Suggests risk premium could return to oil as the dust settles, favoring a bounce.
insights.quote: this has a lot of similarities to what Liberation Day was for equities

insights.claim: Every says the lack of transmission from Hormuz fertilizer disruption into grain prices reflects agricultural season timing, war-duration expectations, stock depletion and demand destruction, but that sustained high sulfur prices and energy disruption could still lift food prices with a lag.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Grain markets may be under-pricing a lagged fertilizer/sulfur shock if disruption persists.

themes.theme: Data center moratoria and the AI trade

insights.claim: Erik Townsend says data center pauses in multiple states, announced by Democrats as a remedy for high electric bills, are nearly certain after the midterms, with some describing the Texas outcome as 'regime change'.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: State-level moratoria directly threaten AI capex buildout and associated power/equipment suppliers.

insights.claim: Every suggests some planned data center buildout may have been washed out anyway because the required water, copper, chips and electricity may not have been available, meaning moratoria partly mask pre-existing fantasy capex.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: AI capex projections may have been overstated independent of politics.

insights.claim: Every argues that if AI really is a Sputnik- or Manhattan Project-style national security race, a Luddite-driven data center pause hands the lead to China, and expects the new Democratic Congress to be briefed on that framing.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: National-security framing may limit how far moratoria go, a potential reversal catalyst for the AI trade.

insights.claim: Townsend observes that nuclear and uranium stocks fell harder than the broad market after the election and stayed down while the market recovered toward its 50-day moving average, despite nuclear being the solution to the power-cost problem driving data center pauses; Every agrees the logic for abundant cheap nuclear power is a necessity that won't go away.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Nuclear/uranium equities may be mispriced by being lumped in with the AI data-center selloff.
insights.quote: whoever has power, electricity, has power

insights.claim: Patrick Ceresna notes that after the election, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon gapped up 5 to 6% while AI infrastructure trades including semiconductors broke to fresh multi-month lows, and the Nasdaq did not participate in the reversal.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Market rotating out of AI infrastructure into hyperscalers; index strength is narrow.

insights.claim: Ceresna concludes the AI trade continues to correct and would only turn meaningfully bullish if the Nasdaq reclaims its 50-day moving average and resumes its trend.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Nasdaq 50-day moving average is the technical trigger to watch for re-risking AI exposure.

themes.theme: Tariffs, blocs and grand macro strategy

insights.claim: Every argues tariffs, alongside industrial policy, are historically the only way to reindustrialize short of equally costly subsidies, so removing them would accelerate the decline of the US as global hegemon by undermining the industrial base behind its military-industrial complex.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Expect tariff regimes to persist in some form even under a hostile Congress; reshoring themes remain intact.
insights.quote: tariffs are historically, as neo-mercantilist history shows, pretty much the only way, alongside other aspects of industrial policy, that you are going to reindustrialize

insights.claim: Every says removing tariffs would lower costs short term but also cut revenue for a government already struggling to raise it and remove leverage for reindustrialization.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Tariff rollback would widen fiscal deficits, relevant for Treasury supply and yields.

insights.claim: Every hypothesizes a post-midterm bargain where Trump removes some tariffs but keeps those on China and offers partners such as Europe, which is close to aggressive new China tariff legislation, a common external tariff with lower internal tariffs, fast-tracking a two-bloc world.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: A US-Europe common China tariff would reshape trade flows and hit China-exposed exporters.
insights.quote: We were in two blocks fairly quickly.

insights.claim: Every frames Trump's trade strategy as building a bloc via USMCA, where Canada is the holdout, and across the Americas, where Brazil is the big holdout.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Canada and Brazil are the key friction points in any Western-hemisphere trade bloc.

insights.claim: Every says his 'grand macro strategy' framework (grand strategy fused with market-facing macro) still describes the White House approach, but the failure on affordability and on winning the war quickly means the strategy must change again after the midterms.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Policy playbooks are shifting; expect pivots toward affordability measures.

insights.claim: Every speculates Trump could revive a floated idea of lottery-allocated free land on federally owned land to build around 10 new cities, linking tariff/bloc policy to the affordability agenda.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Possible housing-supply policy pivot with implications for homebuilders and building inputs.
insights.quote: we're just going to start 10 new cities on federally owned land and lottery style

themes.theme: Washington gridlock, fiscal and political outlook

insights.claim: Every says the market now faces a vastly wider range of probable outcomes than under the prior Trump glide path, where for all the volatility one could narrow down the likely range.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Higher uncertainty argues for elevated volatility pricing across assets.
insights.quote: now we have a glide path with a vastly wider range of probable outcomes

insights.claim: Every warns that rather than benign gridlock, Washington could enter a self-destructive cycle of both sides trying to out-lawyer each other, which would weaken US foreign policy, including its ability to pass armaments funding for the Pentagon.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: The 'gridlock is good for markets' consensus may be wrong if conflict dominates.

insights.claim: Every notes Trump is not a lame duck: he has two years, veto power, executive orders, and potentially Supreme Court support, while the outgoing Congress is already in a lame-duck phase.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Executive actions (tariffs, orders) remain the main policy channel near term.

insights.claim: Every expects possible two-year gridlock but eventually generous Democrat-drafted spending bills, with uncertainty over whether Trump becomes a fiscal hawk or indulges them, determining whether weaker-dollar and gold trades work.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Fiscal path is the swing factor for dollar and gold positioning.

insights.claim: Every says a 2027 debt ceiling standoff in isolation would follow the familiar playbook of days to months until someone blinks, with nothing new for traders.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Debt-ceiling drama alone should be faded rather than treated as a regime event.

insights.claim: Every judges there is a clear possibility of a third party forming from alienated former Trump allies but a 0% probability of it getting near power, and that it acted as a distractor in this election.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Third-party scenarios should not factor into 2028 election positioning.
insights.quote: there's a 0% probability of that getting anywhere near any power

insights.claim: Every says the dollar weakened on uncertainty, noting that whereas geopolitical tension usually sends investors to the dollar, the market now dislikes both geopolitical risk and the absence of Trumpism.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: The dollar's safe-haven reflex may be impaired in a US-politics-driven shock.

themes.theme: Market desk: cross-asset tells and the MPC trade

insights.claim: Patrick Ceresna proposes a Marathon Petroleum (MPC) December 18, 2026 390/450 bull call spread at about a $20 debit with MPC near $392.68, offering $40 max profit (2-to-1) and a $410 breakeven, after a $116 or 23% decline over 16 days back to September lows.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Concrete defined-risk way to express the elevated refining-margin view on a mean-reversion bounce.

insights.claim: Ceresna says the 10-year, 30-year, 2-year Treasury yields and SOFR did not move meaningfully after the election, which he reads as a big tell that bond traders do not see a macro regime change.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Lack of rates confirmation undercuts the disinflation narrative implied by the oil drop.
insights.quote: bond traders are not convinced that something has dynamically changed

insights.claim: Ceresna says the dollar, with the index around 101.18 near multi-month lows, remains in levels seen before the election and still looks like a buy-on-dip, breaking down only if an imminent big peace deal validates the oil sell-off.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Dollar bull trend intact absent a confirmed peace deal.
insights.quote: this still has all the characteristics of a buy on dip

insights.claim: Ceresna views gold's post-election bounce back above $4,000 as an oversold counter-trend after a roughly $900, near-20% two-month drop, since a weak dollar, lower rates and central bank easing backdrop is absent, and he would be skeptical even of a further $100-200 rally.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Treat gold rallies as short-term trades rather than a new bull market.
insights.quote: I don't think that there's any evidence here that a new bull market has started

insights.claim: Ceresna compares the current gold bounce to the August move, when an oversold gold ripped on PBoC 'Operation Twist' news before sellers returned after a few weeks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Historical analog suggests fading gold strength after a few weeks.
